title: National Taiwan University Hospital
paragraphs: I recently studied abroad at National Taiwan University for 12 weeks from March. Because I was originally poor at English, I had not considered studying abroad at all. However, as I advanced through the school years, I began to want to do something that I could only do as a student before graduating, and as I listened to the stories of those who had studied abroad, my longing for study abroad grew stronger, so I decided to go.

Originally, I had heard that Taiwan is a pro-Japanese country, that many Taiwanese people come to Japan every year and that many travelers come from Japan, so I had wanted to go once. And since English is apparently used in most of medicine in Taiwan, I chose National Taiwan University this time because I wanted to learn a lot in the clerkship and also to see with my own eyes what medical education in English in a non-English-speaking country is like.

National Taiwan University Hospital has more than 2,300 beds, and more than 6,500 foreign patients reportedly visit every year. In fact, during my clerkship I had many opportunities to see foreign patients, and each time the doctors examined them in English as if used to it. In that setting, I did clerkships of two to three weeks each in obstetrics and gynecology, dermatology, family medicine, endocrinology and general surgery.

First, in obstetrics and gynecology, the first department, I was allowed to rotate through obstetrics, gynecology and fertility treatment, one week each. In obstetrics I was able to see many deliveries of special cases, such as painless delivery, which is not done much in Japan, and deliveries of children with congenital heart disease. In gynecology, in the morning I observed surgery, and in the afternoon, after taking part in a conference, I did surgical clerkship activities mixed in with the local students. At National Taiwan University, robotic surgery is frequently performed in gynecological surgery, and I was actually allowed to operate the da Vinci. Although robotic surgery in obstetrics and gynecology is not covered by insurance in Taiwan, about three to four robotic operations are reportedly performed a week. In Japan robotic surgery was not much used for gynecological diseases, so I was surprised at the difference and it was a good opportunity to observe robotic surgery. In the surgical clerkship afterward, I did the clerkship mixed in with a group of local students. In the fertility treatment department, the number of patients coming for fertility treatment was very large, and at the end of every day they held a conference about that day's patients, discussing countless patients every day. Many patients reportedly come from Japan too, and I realized the high level.

Dermatology is the most popular department in Taiwan and also covers cosmetic dermatology, so I chose it because I wanted to see what it was like. In fact, apparently only those with top grades each year can become dermatologists. The clerkship was basically outpatient clinic and observing surgery. There was little I could do myself, but I was taught in great detail about dermatological diseases I had seen only in textbooks, and it was very educational. Not only rare diseases, but I was also shocked that, even though it was a university hospital, many patients visited for acne and rough skin. I was also allowed to observe the outpatient clinic of the most famous cosmetic dermatologist in Taiwan, who has launched his own cosmetics brand.

In the next, family medicine, I did clerkships of one week each, divided into general ward, palliative ward and outpatient clinic. On the ward, I was put into a group, went on rounds of patients with a resident in the morning, then discussed their condition while looking at the charts, and in the evening did rounds again with a senior physician. Since the patients could not speak English, I could not take histories myself, but every day I was allowed to take physical findings and so on together with the residents. In the palliative ward, in addition, I was able to learn things I could not learn much in clerkships in Japan, such as psychological care for patients and families and pain management. In the outpatient clinic, I observed outpatient clinics that are rare in Japan, such as palliative, smoking cessation, weight loss and travel clinics, and was taken not only to the university hospital but also to outside clinics and home-visit nursing.

In endocrinology, they arranged the schedule so that I could do a balanced clerkship of ward, outpatient clinic, thyroid ultrasound and so on. Since Taiwan has a large number of diabetes patients, the country actively promotes diabetes screening, and I was shown tests that I had hardly seen in Japan. Also, many advertisements for blood glucose meters were posted on station posters and the like, which I felt told of the large number of diabetes patients. However, in Taiwan not only the number of diabetes patients but also the number of patients with endocrine diseases is tremendous, and about 50 thyroid ultrasounds were performed every day. At the professor's outpatient clinic, about 200 patients a day came, almost all with endocrine diseases, and I was surprised and also able to see many cases.

In the last, general surgery, I basically observed one to three operations of interest each day. Here too, as in gynecology, robotic surgery was performed, and I observed surgery while hearing about the advantages and disadvantages of robotic surgery. Since the clerkship of the new school year began the very week I started rotating, both the doctors and students seemed busy, but they found time to discuss together things like why this patient came to need surgery, and it was very educational.

I would also like to touch on life outside the clerkship. I stayed for three months at Jingfu Hall, a dormitory of National Taiwan University. All the rooms there were twin rooms, and as I had gone alone from Nagoya University, I lived there with another exchange student. At first I was not very keen and even looked for other dormitories. However, when I tried it, talking about our countries with my roommate every night and going out together on days off, I could spend days more enjoyable than living alone. Since there were many exchange students in that dormitory, we went out to dinner together almost every day, sometimes went drinking, and they even held a birthday party for me. I never imagined I could make friends from all over the world while in Taiwan, but thanks to that, without being at a loose end or feeling lonely, the 12 weeks became irreplaceable.

Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to express my gratitude to Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and all the members of the International Collaboration Office and the Frontier Society, and everyone at National Taiwan University, who gave me this valuable opportunity. Thank you very much.
